items.name: Atomic transactions
items.explanation: A transaction bundles several changes into one step: all of them happen or none do, and other readers never see the half-done state. A change that is not committed yet is invisible to other readers.

assumedBy.quote: Next, a write transaction updated both the metadata table and the version table atomically.
Additionally, by using binlogs, we don’t run the risk of letting uncommitted transactions pollute the cache.

items.name: Binary log and change data capture
items.explanation: A MySQL server can keep a binary log of events that describe the changes made to its data, which is how replicas copy it. Uber's Flux reads that log and passes each change to other systems, an approach called change data capture.

assumedBy.quote: Flux tails the MySQL binlog events for each of the clusters in our storage engine layer and publishes the events to a list of consumers.

sources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: The Binary Log

items.name: Redis and atomic Lua scripts
items.explanation: Redis is an in-memory data store, often used as a cache, that holds values under keys. Its EVAL command runs a small Lua script on the server as one uninterrupted step, so a check and a write can happen together.

assumedBy.quote: Redis supports executing custom Lua scripts atomically using the EVAL command.

sources.title: Get started with Redis Open Source

items.name: Latency percentiles (P99, P99.9)
items.explanation: A percentile says what share of requests were at least this fast: P99 is the time that 99 out of 100 requests beat, so it shows the slow tail that an average hides. P99.9 and P99.99 look further into that tail. The SRE book's example is a service averaging 100 ms where 1% of requests take 5 seconds.

assumedBy.quote: P75 latency is down 75% and P99.9 latency is down over 67% while also limiting latency spikes, as seen above.

sources.title: Monitoring Distributed Systems (Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 6)

items.name: Eventual and strong consistency
items.explanation: Strong consistency means every read sees the latest write; eventual consistency means the copies agree after a delay.

assumedBy.quote: “Cache should eventually be consistent with the database” is a typical client-observable invariant that Polaris monitors, especially in the presence of asynchronous cache invalidation.
Docstore is a strongly consistent database.

items.name: Sharding and shard keys
items.explanation: Splitting one big dataset across many databases by a key, so each holds only part of it.

assumedBy.quote: Additionally, data is sharded across multiple partitions containing one leader and two follower nodes using Raft for consensus.

items.name: Publish-subscribe
items.explanation: A way to announce that something changed so every interested service hears about it, without the sender knowing who they are.

assumedBy.quote: Something (e.g., a client or a pub/sub system) needs to tell the cache that a mutation happened.

items.name: Circuit breaker
items.explanation: A guard that stops calling a service that keeps failing, so calls fail fast instead of piling up.

assumedBy.quote: If a Redis node goes down, we’d like to be able to short circuit requests to that node to avoid the unnecessary latency penalty of a Redis get/set request for which we have high confidence that it will fail.

items.name: Consensus (Raft, Paxos)
items.explanation: Several machines agreeing on one order of changes even when some fail, with Raft and Paxos as two named ways to do it.

assumedBy.quote: The storage engine layer is responsible for consensus via Raft, replication, transactions, concurrency control, and load management.
